risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree - serious: contemporaneous firm-level OLS with no lags, no instrument and an author admission that none was found.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree - critical: the 'AI' variable is built only from innovation items and the text calls it a 'proxy of innovation-related variables', so it cannot capture AI adoption (a measure that misses the exposure is at least serious; here it is total).
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree - serious: ten countries chosen as 'growing economies in terms of GDP' with no rule, panel structure and years per country unstated (reviewer 1 asks how firms are tracked), Nigeria about 46 percent of observations.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree - serious: growth formulas are garbled in the text and Table 1 (min 0.927, max 195.32; sales growth range 1 to 36.283), and sales growth is a regressor for labour productivity growth, which is built from sales.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree - serious: controls vary by table, the FGLS/OLS labelling is inconsistent, HDFE absorbed dimension is not stated, and many size, country and industry models are run without multiple-testing handling.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree - serious: abstract and conclusion state positive AI effects while the HDFE pooled labour productivity effect is insignificant, text signs contradict or cannot be matched to tables, and Table 7 col (1) duplicates Table 5 col (1).
risk_of_bias.why: Critical overall is defensible because the exposure is not AI, there is no identification, and the reporting has internal inconsistencies that prevent trusting even the associations.

problems: No invented numbers found; every table value cited in the record matches the text. Points to carry: (1) The Table 4 caption says robust OLS while the text says column (1) is FGLS. (2) The converted text loses minus signs, so the record's directions for country and size results rest on the narrative text, not the tables; the text contradicts the tables in places (Kenya, Ethiopia, South Africa, micro HDFE). (3) The record says Table 1 'minimums/signs unclear'; this is right (AI index min 1.441 and IA min 1.622 are printed unsigned). (4) Table 13 cols (1)-(2) vs Table 4 col (1) give very different AI coefficients on the same N, which the record notes only as 'not comparable'. (5) Reviewers do ask for justification of the AI index and for formulas, as the record says; the record's page range for reviewer reports (pp.18-21) is right.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: too_harsh - moderate: the authors disclaim causal interpretation ('conditional associations rather than causal effects') and state the exogeneity and Nickell issues openly, though no strategy is applied.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree - moderate: PCA of internet, broadband and ICT exports is a sensible ICT index; the green half of the interaction is contaminated by biomass.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: too_harsh - moderate: the 17 economies come from a stated, pre-estimation rule (at least 10 years of survey data, no gap over 3 years); the real limits are small subgroup N and the Asia-Pacific focus.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree - serious: informality is own-account plus contributing family workers, excluding informal wage work; productivity is an ILO modelled estimate.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree - serious: Nickell bias uncorrected, subgroup models have no year FE while the pooled model reverses the sign, 4 to 6 clusters, static threshold model, no leave-one-out.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree - moderate: nulls and the sign reversal are reported, but the Conclusions still say the synergy 'holds specifically and strongly' and productivity synergy is 'robustly' positive.
risk_of_bias.why: Serious overall holds because the informality proxy is narrow, the central subgroup result does not survive the authors' own pooled test and the inference rests on 4 to 6 clusters; the transparency of the authors keeps it from critical.

problems: No invented numbers. The text contains revision-round residue ('requested in Round 3', 'the reviewer's concern'), which does not change the numbers. The Conclusions' wording ('holds specifically and strongly', 'robustly and positively synergistic') is stronger than the results and Section 5.4, as the record says. The record's 'DIGI x GREEN lower-middle subgroup uses 60 obs, entity FE only' is correct (Table 6 note). Labour productivity in Model 5 is a level, not growth, as recorded.

eligibility_note: Own system-GMM estimation, 32 economies (18 OECD, 14 MENA), exposures internet, mobile, fixed telephone and ICT imports, outcome GDP growth (output). Eligible, although the dependent variable is inconsistently defined (see problems).

The record's 'no low-income' is not supported by the text (Syria is on the MENA list and is World Bank low-income by external classification), and its remark on OECD members being 'high/upper-middle' is not from the paper.

income_group_note: The paper reports no income-group results; OECD vs MENA is a region split. Filling 'high' with OECD results is the extractor's mapping, and the 'none in sample' for low income is unsupported (see sample correction). Better to record all four income groups as not reported and keep the region contrast under heterogeneity.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree - serious: system GMM with internal instruments is the only strategy, diagnostics are weak (Sargan p up to 1.000, AR2 p of 0.06 to 0.10 in all four MENA models and 0.0172 in Table 10 spec 1, 0.0803 in Table 9 spec 4), causal language throughout. Also missing from the record: OECD models use 19 instruments for 18 countries.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree - moderate: coarse penetration and import-share indicators, one ICT variable per model.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: agree - serious: unexplained selection of 18 of 38 OECD members and 14 MENA economies including conflict cases, very unbalanced (156 and 73 observations), short window including COVID.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree - serious: equation says growth of real GDP but tables carry L.log_PIB and the text says 'output per capita lagged'. The OECD mean of TX_PIB is -0.374 (min -16.78, max 13.07), implausible for real GDP growth of 18 OECD members over 2010-2023. The record's remark that MENA max 121.78 is implausible is weaker: conflict economies can show such values, but the definition is still unclear.
risk_of_bias.specification: agree - serious: four ICT variables entered separately across six tables, text misreports significance in places (e.g. 'four scenarios' for OECD but only three columns), threshold rule contradicted by the author's own results.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree - serious: Table 5 omits the OECD internet specification, abstract and conclusion state ICT promotes growth although most MENA ICT coefficients are null.
risk_of_bias.why: The cumulative problems (outcome not reconcilable with its definition, an omitted headline specification, instrument count above group count in OECD models, text contradicting tables) mean the OECD-vs-MENA conclusion cannot be relied on, which fits critical rather than serious.

problems: No invented numbers. Issues to carry: (1) 'two-step' in the record's estimator cannot be confirmed because the Table 5 note is truncated ('stage Generalized Method of Moments'). (2) The record's country lists, years and observation counts (156, 73) are right; the text says the model includes both country and year effects, with no coefficients shown. (3) The record places OECD under 'high income' and states no low-income economies; the paper does not classify income. (4) Direction 'mixed' for result 8 should be 'not reported'. (5) Text claim 'OECD fixed telephone, internet, mobile all positive in interaction with credit' is true only at 10 percent for fixed telephone (p=0.091).

eligibility_note: Own panel estimation, 27 EU members plus the EU aggregate (28 units), ICT exposure via the DESI composite, outcome TFP (productivity). Meets the at-least-10-economies rule; no income-group comparison is needed.

income_group_note: Paper has no income-group analysis; the record already says income groups are not separated, so only the empty 'high' note is an inference.

risk_of_bias.confounding_reverse_causation: agree - serious: causal language ('It can be assumed that the model proves the causal effect'), country FE only, no lags or instruments, no year effects, so common shocks and trends are uncontrolled.
risk_of_bias.exposure_measurement: agree - moderate: DESI is a broad composite with human capital and public services, plausible ICT index for EU.
risk_of_bias.selection_of_countries_years: too_harsh - moderate: the sample is the full EU-27 for the whole period DESI exists, not a selected set; the real defects are only six years and the EU aggregate entered as a unit alongside its members.
risk_of_bias.outcome_measurement: agree - moderate: TFP is an author-built Cobb-Douglas residual with alpha and capital series not reported; the text calls it labour productivity growth.
risk_of_bias.specification: too_lenient - serious: no year effects in a 2017-2022 panel with a trending index and the COVID shock, conventional (apparently unclustered) t-statistics despite rho_ar of 0.28 to 0.51, only six time points, headline loses significance in the fullest model.
risk_of_bias.selective_reporting: agree - moderate: the abstract and conclusion state 0.1 percent as 'proved' without noting the null in col (4), though the null is disclosed in the body.
risk_of_bias.why: Serious overall is right: causal claim from a two-way-less FE regression on 28 units over six years, with the headline coefficient not robust to adding institutions.

problems: The record's statement 'Some table inconsistencies (Table 1 vs Table 2 constants)' is not supported: Table 1 lnTFP column and Table 2 col (1) give identical coefficients and constant (4.941). The only different constant is for the TFP_ind column in Table 1 (-1.373), which has a different dependent variable. Other facts check out: 168 observations, 28 units, 140 observations in FE-AR models, rho_ar values. The Table 3 col (1) header says Durbin-Watson test but it reports rho_ar, so it is an AR(1) FE estimator.
